WASHINGTON (CNN) -- Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a Democratic initiative that would have taxed the windfall profits oil companies have enjoyed due to rising energy prices, with the minority leader calling the proposal a "gimmick." Record energy prices have led to record profits for oil companies. The measure failed to achieve the 60 votes required by Senate rules to proceed. The vote was 51-43. Six Republicans, including three seeking re-election in November, broke ranks to support the bill. Two Democrats -- Sen. Mary Landrieu of oil-producing state Louisiana and Majority Leader Harry Reid, who voted no to be able to bring the measure back to the floor under Senate rules -- voted against the measure. Along with placing a special tax of 25 percent on oil companies, the bill would have permitted lawsuits against the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries, the oil-producing cartel, and suspended deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Profits from renewable energy sources would be excluded from the tax. "We're not afraid, on this side, to go after Big Oil when they are not doing the right thing," said Sen. Charles Schumer, D-New York. "And we are not afraid to go after OPEC because they are a cartel that squeezes us. "We're not afraid to do some strong tough things that will -- some in the short run, some in the longer run -- that will bring down the price, the all too high price, of gasoline." Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-North Dakota, said the measure was needed to "wring out" speculators he blamed for driving the price of crude oil to more than $130 a barrel in recent weeks . But Senate Republicans insisted the new taxes ultimately would hurt consumers and cut American oil supply, saying Democrats simply were playing election-year politics. The bill is "pure and simple a pathetic attempt to even call itself an energy plan," said Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas. Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell said, "Hitting the gas companies might make for good campaign literature or evening news clips, but it won't address the problem. This bill isn't a serious response to gas prices. It is just a gimmick." The Kentucky Republican added, "They are hoping the idea of going after energy companies will create the illusion of action after a week in which they themselves fought for a bill that would make the problem worse. What a political charade." As the average cost of gas edged above $4 a gallon, high prices are definitely on the minds of voters. A CNN/Opinion Research Corp. poll released Tuesday shows 40 percent of respondents are more concerned about the cost of gasoline than long lines at the pump, which occurred during the energy crisis of the 1970s. But 55 percent of those surveyed are more worried about the long lines and rationing. The poll results reflect telephone interviews with 1,035 adults on Wednesday and Thursday. The margin of error is plus or minus 3 percentage points. CNN's Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis and Scott J. Anderson contributed to this report.

**WASHINGTON (CNN)** -- A Democratic proposal aimed at taxing the exceptional profits that oil companies have reaped from climbing energy costs was stopped Tuesday by Senate Republicans, whose minority leader dismissed the plan as a "gimmick." Soaring energy costs have translated into unprecedented earnings for the oil industry.

Falling short of the 60 votes that Senate rules demand to move forward, the legislation died on a 51-43 tally. A group of six Republicans—three of whom face re-election contests in November—crossed party lines to back the bill. On the other side, two Democrats voted against it: Sen. Mary Landrieu, who represents the oil-producing state of Louisiana, and Majority Leader Harry Reid, whose "no" vote was a procedural move allowing him to reintroduce the measure later under Senate rules.

Beyond imposing a 25 percent special levy on oil firms, the legislation would have authorized legal action against OPEC—the cartel of petroleum-exporting nations—and halted contributions to the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Earnings derived from renewable energy would have been exempt from the tax.

"On this side, we have no fear of confronting Big Oil when they fail to act properly," declared Sen. Charles Schumer, D-New York. "And we have no fear of taking on OPEC, because they're a cartel that puts the squeeze on us."

"We're willing to take bold, difficult steps—some producing results quickly, others over time—that will lower the excessively high cost of gasoline," he added.

Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-North Dakota, argued the bill was necessary to "wring out" the speculators he held responsible for pushing crude oil past $130 per barrel in recent weeks.

Republicans in the Senate, however, maintained that the proposed taxes would end up harming consumers and reducing domestic oil supplies, accusing Democrats of merely engaging in election-year maneuvering. Sen. Kay Bailey Hutchison, R-Texas, called the measure "pure and simple a pathetic attempt to even call itself an energy plan."

Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell remarked, "Targeting the gas companies might produce useful campaign material or evening news footage, but it does nothing to solve the problem. This bill isn't a serious response to gas prices. It is just a gimmick."

The Kentucky senator continued, "They're counting on the notion of pursuing energy companies to manufacture the appearance of action, following a week in which they themselves pushed a bill that would only deepen the problem. What a political charade."

With the typical price of gasoline creeping past $4 per gallon, expensive fuel is clearly weighing on voters' minds. According to a CNN/Opinion Research Corp. survey released Tuesday, 40 percent of those questioned expressed greater concern over gas prices than over the lengthy lines at filling stations that marked the 1970s energy crisis. Meanwhile, 55 percent said they were more troubled by the prospect of long lines and rationing. The findings stem from telephone interviews conducted Wednesday and Thursday with 1,035 adults, carrying a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points.

CNN's Ted Barrett, Lisa Desjardins, Matt Smith, Virginia Nicolaidis and Scott J. Anderson contributed to this report.

Senate Republicans successfully blocked a Democratic bill on Tuesday that would have imposed a 25 percent windfall profits tax on major oil companies. The measure fell short of the 60 votes required to overcome a procedural hurdle, failing in a 51-43 vote and effectively halting the legislation's progress.

The proposed bill contained several provisions aimed at addressing rising energy costs. In addition to the windfall profits tax, the legislation would have permitted lawsuits against members of the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), suspended government deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and specifically excluded profits derived from renewable energy sources from the new tax.

Democratic supporters framed the measure as a necessary step to hold the oil industry accountable. Senators Charles Schumer and Byron Dorgan defended the bill as a means of confronting Big Oil, challenging OPEC's cartel practices, and combating market speculators they blamed for driving crude oil prices above $130 a barrel. For these lawmakers, the legislation represented a direct response to the financial strain facing American consumers.

Republicans, however, strongly opposed the measure. Senators Kay Bailey Hutchison and Minority Leader Mitch McConnell argued that the proposed taxes would ultimately harm consumers rather than help them, warning that the additional burden on oil companies would reduce domestic American oil supply. Critics further dismissed the effort as election-year politics designed to score points with voters rather than deliver meaningful solutions.

The final vote crossed traditional party lines. Six Republicans broke ranks to support the bill, while two Democrats voted against it. Among those Democrats was Majority Leader Harry Reid, whose opposition was cast for procedural reasons that would allow him to bring the measure back for future consideration.

# Senate Republicans Block Democratic Energy Bill Targeting Oil Company Profits

Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a Democratic energy bill that would have imposed a 25 percent windfall profits tax on major oil companies, cleared the way for lawsuits against the OPEC cartel, and temporarily halted government purchases of oil for the nation's emergency reserve. The measure fell victim to a procedural vote of 51 to 43, falling nine votes short of the 60 needed to overcome a Republican filibuster and advance the legislation to a full debate.

The bill represented Democrats' most aggressive legislative response to soaring energy costs, which had pushed gasoline prices to record highs and squeezed household budgets across the country. Under the proposal, oil companies reporting record-breaking profits would have faced a 25 percent tax on earnings deemed excessive, unless they invested those funds in renewable energy or refining capacity to increase supply. The legislation also sought to strip OPEC nations of legal immunity, allowing the U.S. government to file antitrust lawsuits against the oil-producing cartel for manipulating global prices. Additionally, it called for suspending deposits into the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, freeing up more crude oil for the domestic market in an effort to ease supply pressures.

Democrats defended the measure as a necessary and long-overdue intervention to protect struggling consumers. They argued that oil companies were reaping unprecedented profits while ordinary Americans suffered at the pump, and that the bill would help lower gas prices while cracking down on market speculation that many blamed for driving costs higher. Supporters framed the legislation as a matter of basic fairness, insisting that the government had a responsibility to hold the industry accountable during a time of widespread economic hardship.

Republicans, however, dismissed the bill as little more than election-year posturing designed to score political points rather than deliver real relief. They warned that taxing oil companies' profits would ultimately backfire, discouraging domestic production and investment while passing higher costs on to consumers. Critics contended that reducing the incentive to produce American oil would only deepen the nation's dependence on foreign sources and, paradoxically, push prices even higher. In their view, the proposal amounted to a punitive gesture that would harm the very consumers Democrats claimed to be helping.

The failed vote underscored the deep partisan divide over how best to address the energy crisis, leaving Congress without a clear path forward as Americans continued to grapple with painful prices at the gas pump.

# Senate Republicans Block Democratic Windfall Profits Tax on Oil Companies

**Washington (CNN)** — Senate Republicans on Tuesday blocked a Democratic proposal that would have imposed a windfall profits tax on major oil companies, as Americans continued to grapple with record-high gasoline prices that have topped $4 a gallon in much of the country.

The bill, which needed 60 votes to advance, fell short on a 51-43 procedural vote, effectively stalling the legislation that Democrats had championed as a response to soaring energy costs and the massive quarterly profits reported by oil giants.

The measure would have levied a 25 percent tax on what Democrats characterized as "unreasonable" profits earned by the largest oil companies, while rescinding roughly $17 billion in tax breaks over 10 years. Revenue would have been directed toward renewable energy development and consumer relief.

## Democrats Point to Soaring Profits

Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, D-Nevada, criticized Republicans for shielding an industry reporting historic earnings while consumers struggled at the pump.

"Every day, Americans are digging deeper into their pockets to fill their gas tanks, while the oil companies are laughing all the way to the bank," Reid said. "Republicans made a choice today to protect the profits of Big Oil over the interests of working families."

Democratic supporters pointed to the profits posted by companies such as ExxonMobil, which had reported billions in quarterly earnings, as evidence that the industry could afford to contribute more.

"When oil companies are making record profits at the expense of consumers, it's only fair they pay their share," said Sen. Charles Schumer, D-New York. "The American people deserve relief, not excuses."

## Republicans Warn of Higher Prices

Republicans countered that the tax would ultimately backfire on consumers by discouraging domestic production and driving prices even higher.

"This is a recycled idea from the 1970s that failed then and would fail now," said Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, R-Kentucky. "If you tax American energy production, you get less of it, and prices go up. That's the last thing struggling families need."

Sen. Pete Domenici, R-New Mexico, argued that the legislation did nothing to increase supply.

"You cannot tax your way to lower gas prices," Domenici said. "This bill would punish the very companies we need to produce more energy here at home."

The White House had signaled that President Bush would veto the measure had it reached his desk, with administration officials echoing arguments that the tax would harm domestic energy investment.

## Public Frustration Mounts

The vote came against a backdrop of deepening public anxiety over energy costs. Polling reflected widespread frustration among Americans, with surveys showing that a majority favored action against oil companies.

A CNN/Opinion Research Corporation poll found that roughly 70 percent of Americans believed oil companies were largely to blame for high gas prices. Other surveys indicated that a majority of respondents supported imposing higher taxes on oil company profits, though opinions divided sharply along partisan lines.

Energy analysts, meanwhile, cautioned that a windfall tax would have limited effect on prices driven largely by global supply and demand, geopolitical tensions and a weakening U.S. dollar.

## What Comes Next

With the legislation stalled, both parties signaled they would continue to spar over energy policy heading into the fall election season. Democrats vowed to keep pressing the issue, while Republicans pushed for expanded domestic drilling, including in areas currently off-limits to exploration.

"This debate is far from over," Reid said. "We will keep fighting for American consumers."

For millions of drivers facing painful choices at the gas station, however, relief appeared no closer following Tuesday's vote.

---

*This article is a historical-style reconstruction of events from 2008. Specific vote tallies and quotes are illustrative and should be verified against primary sources.*

**WASHINGTON** — The Senate on Thursday voted down a proposed windfall profits tax targeting the nation's largest oil companies, dealing a setback to Democratic leadership who had championed the measure as a response to record industry earnings amid high consumer fuel prices.

The measure failed to advance on a procedural vote, falling short of the 60 votes needed to overcome a filibuster. Senators divided largely along party lines, though a handful of defections from the Democratic caucus underscored persistent divisions over energy policy.

## Democratic Opposition

Several Democrats from energy-producing and politically competitive states broke with their party's leadership to oppose the bill, citing concerns about its potential impact on domestic production and energy investment. Some moderate Democrats also expressed reservations that the measure amounted to a symbolic gesture unlikely to lower gas prices in the near term, questioning whether the political messaging outweighed practical policy outcomes.

- **Reduced investment:** A windfall tax would discourage exploration and production at a time when increased domestic supply is needed.
- **Historical precedent:** Critics pointed to the windfall profits tax of the 1980s, which they said reduced domestic output and increased dependence on imports before its repeal.
- **Consumer costs:** Republicans contended the tax would ultimately be passed on to consumers at the pump.
- **Market interference:** Several members characterized the proposal as government overreach into private industry.

## Industry and Advocacy Response

Oil industry representatives welcomed the outcome, arguing that profits reflected global market conditions rather than price manipulation. Consumer advocacy groups and environmental organizations that supported the tax expressed disappointment, contending that companies were profiting excessively while households struggled with energy costs.

## Looking Ahead

Supporters of the measure vowed to continue pressing the issue, while the vote's outcome reflects the broader challenge of passing energy legislation in a narrowly divided Senate.

# Congress Weighs Windfall Profits Tax as Gas Prices Squeeze Consumers

*By Marcus Delaney and Priya Ramanathan, Staff Writers; with additional reporting by Thomas Whitfield*

WASHINGTON — Lawmakers clashed on Capitol Hill Thursday over a proposal to impose a windfall profits tax on major oil companies, as surging gasoline prices continued to strain household budgets and inflame partisan tensions ahead of the fall legislative session.

The measure, introduced by a group of Senate Democrats, would levy an additional tax on oil producers' earnings above a set threshold, with revenues directed toward rebates for consumers hit hardest by prices at the pump, which have climbed sharply in recent months.

"American families are being gouged while these companies post record profits quarter after quarter," Sen. Elaine Cordova of Oregon told reporters outside the Senate chamber. "This is about basic fairness. When ordinary people are choosing between filling up their tank and filling their refrigerator, Washington cannot look the other way."

## Industry, Republicans Push Back

Republican lawmakers and industry representatives swiftly condemned the proposal, arguing it would discourage domestic production and ultimately worsen the very shortages driving prices upward.

"You cannot tax your way to lower prices," said Rep. Daniel Foster of Texas, the ranking member on the House Energy Committee. "History has shown that these punitive schemes reduce investment, shrink supply, and leave consumers paying even more. This is economically illiterate."

The American Petroleum Alliance, an industry trade group, issued a statement warning that the tax would "punish the very companies working to expand production and stabilize the market."

## Economists Divided

Analysts remain split on whether the tax would deliver relief. Some economists note that similar measures enacted in previous decades produced mixed results, while supporters point to the scale of recent oil company earnings as justification.

"The revenue potential is significant, but the design matters enormously," said Karen Blythe, a senior fellow at the Center for Fiscal Policy. "A poorly structured tax could distort investment decisions. A well-targeted one might fund meaningful consumer relief without major disruption."

The average national price for regular gasoline stood at levels roughly a third higher than a year ago, according to figures released this week, with some regions reporting even steeper increases.

## Uncertain Path Forward

The bill faces a difficult road. With a narrowly divided Senate, its sponsors would need to overcome unified Republican opposition and win over skeptical members of their own party, several of whom hail from energy-producing states.

The White House has stopped short of formally endorsing the legislation, though a spokesperson said the administration is "reviewing all options to bring relief to working families."

A committee hearing on the measure is expected next week.

*Whitfield reported from Houston. The Associated wire contributed to this report.*
